lines.text: A small, low country won from the sea, that once traded with the whole world. This is the story of the Netherlands, from canal city to modern Europe.
By about 1300 a town had grown up at a dam on the Amstel. Amsterdam, a city of canals, would one day be the trading centre of the world.
William the Silent, Prince of Orange, would lead the Dutch against Spain, and is still called the father of the fatherland.
In 1568 the provinces rose against their Spanish king, and began a war for freedom that would last eighty years.
Out of the revolt grew a republic of seven provinces, which became rich on trade and a great power at sea.
This was the beginning of the Netherlands as a country of its own, a low-lying land that broke away from Spain.
In 1581 the provinces declared, in plain words, that they no longer obeyed the king of Spain.
In 1602 the Dutch East India Company was founded, selling shares to the public. Its fleets and forts would dominate the spice trade of Asia.
In Amsterdam, Rembrandt painted with bold light and deep shadow, and left behind more than eighty portraits of himself.
Across the Atlantic, Dutch traders founded New Amsterdam on Manhattan. When the English took it in 1664, it became New York.
Christiaan Huygens found Saturn's moon Titan, explained its rings, argued that light is a wave, and built the first accurate pendulum clock.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth merchant, ground tiny lenses and became the first person ever to see bacteria.
In Delft, Johannes Vermeer painted quiet rooms lit from a window. He made few pictures and was almost forgotten for two centuries.
Baruch Spinoza argued that God and nature are one and the same, ideas so bold his own community in Amsterdam expelled him.
In the 1630s the price of tulip bulbs soared to astonishing heights, then crashed, the most famous early bubble of them all.
In 1642 Rembrandt finished The Night Watch, a militia company bursting into motion, now the pride of the Rijksmuseum.
In 1648, at Munster, Spain at last recognised Dutch independence. The eighty years' war was over.
Around 1665 Vermeer painted a girl in a blue and yellow headscarf glancing over her shoulder, the Girl with a Pearl Earring.
In 1713 the peace that ended the War of the Spanish Succession was signed in the Dutch city of Utrecht.
After Napoleon's fall the country became a kingdom under the House of Orange in 1815. Belgium broke away fifteen years later.
Vincent van Gogh made about two thousand works in barely a decade, sold very few, and died at thirty-seven, now one of the best-loved painters ever.
In 1891 Philips began making light bulbs in Eindhoven, and would go on to give the world the cassette and the CD.
In 1900 Ajax was founded in Amsterdam. In the early seventies its Total Football won three European Cups in a row.
Anne Frank kept a diary while her family hid from the Nazis in Amsterdam. She died in a camp, but her words reached the world.
In May 1940 German bombers destroyed the heart of Rotterdam, and the country was occupied.
In the last winter of the war, about twenty thousand people starved to death in the occupied west.
After the war the United Nations' highest court made its home in The Hague.
Johan Cruyff became the star of Ajax and of the national team of the seventies, and later shaped the way Barcelona plays.
In 1953 a storm broke the dikes and the sea drowned more than eighteen hundred people.
The answer was the Delta Works, a great system of dams and storm barriers built over four decades to hold back the North Sea.
Dick Schoof, a former civil servant, would become prime minister in 2024.
In 1984 ASML was founded in Veldhoven. Today its machines print the most advanced computer chips in the world.
In 1992, in the Dutch city of Maastricht, Europe signed the treaty that created the European Union.
And in 2001 the Netherlands became the first country in the world to let same-sex couples marry.
From the canals of Amsterdam to the barriers against the sea, the Dutch kept making their own land and their own way.
